sections.title: A proposal that turns into a fight

blocks.title: He came to propose, and argued about a meadow
blocks.body:
A nervous young landowner puts on his evening dress and goes to his neighbour's house to ask for the daughter's hand. But before he can say the words, the two of them are shouting about who owns a meadow, and then whose dog is better!

**The Proposal** is a comic one-act play by **Anton Chekhov** that laughs at people who care more about property and pride than about love.

blocks.title: The playwright
blocks.body: **Anton Pavlovich Chekhov** was a Russian doctor and one of the greatest writers of short stories and plays. He wrote with gentle humour about ordinary people. The Proposal (1888–89) is a **farce**, a comedy built on exaggerated characters and ridiculous situations, which satirises the 19th-century Russian landowning class and marriages made for property.
blocks.future: Playwrights, actors and screenwriters study Chekhov to learn how to build comedy from character.

blocks.question: Why does Lomov want to marry Natalya, according to his own words?
options: She is a good housekeeper, not bad-looking, well educated, and he needs to marry at 35
He is deeply in love with her
blocks.explanation: His reasons are practical, not romantic, which is part of the satire.

blocks.title: What happens
blocks.body:
**Lomov arrives:** Lomov comes to Chubukov's house in **evening dress**. Chubukov, suspicious at first that he has come to borrow money, is overjoyed when Lomov says he wants to ask for Natalya's hand: 'I've always loved you, my angel, as if you were my own son.' He goes to call Natalya.

**Lomov's nerves:** alone, Lomov worries: he is **35**, a 'critical age'; Natalya is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking and well educated. He suffers from **palpitations**, his **foot goes numb**, his **eyebrow twitches** and he cannot sleep.

**The first quarrel, Oxen Meadows:** Natalya enters in an apron, thinking he has come on business. Lomov starts to explain his family's connection with hers and mentions that his **Oxen Meadows** touch her birchwoods. Natalya says the Meadows are **hers**. They argue hotly; Chubukov joins in, and they hurl insults at each other ('intriguer', 'pettifogger', grandfathers who drank and played cards). Lomov leaves, clutching his heart.

**The truth comes out:** Chubukov tells Natalya that Lomov had come to **propose**. Natalya becomes hysterical: 'Bring him back! Back!' Chubukov fetches him.

**The second quarrel, the dogs:** Natalya, now careful, changes the subject to hunting, but they soon quarrel over whose dog is better: Lomov's **Guess** or Chubukov's **Squeezer**. Lomov says Squeezer is **overshot**; Natalya says Guess is old and ugly. Chubukov joins in again. Lomov collapses into an armchair; Chubukov thinks he is **dead**.

**The 'happy' ending:** Lomov revives. Chubukov makes them kiss and declares, 'She's willing!' and calls for **champagne**. But within moments they are arguing about the dogs again, and Chubukov shouts, 'Champagne!' to drown them out. The marriage is fixed, but the quarrels will clearly continue.

blocks.title: The characters
blocks.body:
| Character | Who | Traits |
|---|---|---|
| **Ivan Vassilevitch Lomov** | a neighbour of Chubukov, a large and hearty but very suspicious landowner, 35 | nervous, a hypochondriac (palpitations, numb foot, twitching eyebrow), quarrelsome |
| **Stepan Stepanovitch Chubukov** | a landowner | hypocritical and greedy: welcomes Lomov warmly, then insults him; wants his daughter married off |
| **Natalya Stepanovna** | Chubukov's daughter, 25 | sharp-tongued, quarrelsome, possessive about property; desperate to marry when she learns of the proposal |

blocks.question: What did Chubukov first suspect Lomov had come for?
blocks.explanation: He resolved not to give it.
option_feedback: He did not guess at first.

blocks.question: What is Lomov's complaint about his health?
options: palpitations, a numb foot, a twitching eyebrow and sleeplessness
blocks.explanation: He is very nervous and easily excited.

blocks.title: Why the play is funny
blocks.body:
**Satire:** the play mocks the **landowning class** of 19th-century Russia, for whom marriage was a matter of **property** and convenience. Lomov proposes for practical reasons; Chubukov wants to marry off his daughter; Natalya wants a husband, but not at the cost of losing a meadow.

**Farce:** exaggerated characters and situations: a man fainting over a dog, a father who swings from 'my angel' to 'intriguer' in minutes, a woman who screams 'Bring him back!'

**Irony:** a proposal, meant to bring two families together, makes them fight; the 'happy ending' is followed at once by another quarrel.

**Character contrast:** all three are **quarrelsome**, proud and stubborn, which is why Chubukov says, 'Here begins the period of conjugal bliss!' The joke is that their marriage will be one long argument.

blocks.title: The two quarrels
blocks.body:
| | First quarrel | Second quarrel |
|---|---|---|
| **About** | **Oxen Meadows** | the dogs **Guess** (Lomov's) and **Squeezer** (Chubukov's) |
| **Lomov says** | the meadows are his; his aunt's grandmother gave the peasants of Natalya's grandfather free use of them | Guess is the better dog; he paid **125 roubles** for him |
| **Natalya says** | the meadows have always belonged to her family | Squeezer is better; Guess is **overshot** (lower jaw shorter than the upper) |
| **Result** | Chubukov joins in, insults Lomov, who leaves; then Natalya learns he came to propose and demands he be brought back | Lomov collapses; Chubukov makes them kiss and agree to marry, and they start quarrelling again |

blocks.question: What are the two quarrels about?
options: a wedding date and a dowry
Oxen Meadows and the dogs Guess and Squeezer
blocks.explanation: Both show their pride and possessiveness.

blocks.question: The Proposal is best described as:
options: a farce that satirises marriage for property
blocks.explanation: Exaggeration and quarrels drive the humour.
option_feedback: Love is the last thing on their minds.

blocks.title: Words and expressions to know
blocks.body:
| Word or phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **hypochondriac** | a person who always worries about being ill |
| **palpitations** | a fast, strong heartbeat |
| **overshot** | (of a dog) with the lower jaw shorter than the upper |
| **intriguer** | a person who plots secretly |
| **pettifogger** | a person who argues over trivial things |
| **conjugal bliss** | married happiness (said ironically) |
| **evening dress** | formal clothes for a special occasion |

**Stage directions** in brackets (for example *[Kisses him]*, *[Faints]*) show actions and add to the comedy.

blocks.question: 'Here begins the period of conjugal bliss!' is said:
options: at the start of the play
ironically, as the couple starts quarrelling again
sincerely, as they are very happy
blocks.explanation: Their married life will be full of quarrels.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Three characters: Lomov (35, nervous), Chubukov (father), Natalya (25).**
- **Two quarrels: Meadows, then Dogs (Guess vs Squeezer).**
- **Lomov's body: heart (palpitations), foot (numb), eyebrow (twitch).**
- **Guess cost 125 roubles; Squeezer is 'overshot'.**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying Lomov proposed at once: he never gets to propose properly; the meadows come first.
2. Mixing up the dogs: **Guess** is Lomov's, **Squeezer** is Chubukov's.
3. Calling it a love story: it is a **farce** and **satire** on marriages for property.
4. Forgetting the ending: they are engaged but quarrelling again.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Perform the second quarrel as a three-person reading. Students mark every stage direction and act it out; then discuss how the actions make the scene funny.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Have you seen people argue over something small and forget what really matters? What does the play suggest about pride?

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Footprints without Feet:** another comic look at human behaviour.
- **History (Rise of Nationalism in Europe):** 19th-century landed aristocracy in Europe.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'The Proposal is a satire on the landowning class of Russia.' Explain in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** Chekhov uses The Proposal to laugh at rich landowners who value property above feelings. Lomov wants to marry Natalya not out of love but because, at 35, he needs a wife, and she is a good housekeeper and not bad-looking. Chubukov is eager to get his daughter married and is friendly only while it suits him. Yet as soon as Lomov mentions Oxen Meadows, all three forget the proposal and fight bitterly over a small piece of land, and then over which dog is better. Insults about grandfathers and family follow. Even after the engagement they quarrel again. The play shows that pride and possessiveness make these people ridiculous, and that marriages based on property are unlikely to be happy.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Lomov, a nervous 35-year-old landowner, comes in evening dress to propose to Natalya, his neighbour Chubukov's daughter.
- Before proposing he quarrels with Natalya over Oxen Meadows; Chubukov joins in and Lomov leaves.
- Learning he came to propose, Natalya demands he be brought back; they then quarrel over the dogs Guess and Squeezer.
- Lomov faints; on reviving he is made to kiss Natalya; they are engaged but begin quarrelling again.
- The play is a farce satirising marriage for property and the pride of landowners.

blocks.title: Exam tips
blocks.body:
- Keep the order of events: arrival, nerves, meadows quarrel, truth, dogs quarrel, faint, engagement, new quarrel.
- Use the words farce, satire and irony in long answers.
- Character sketches: two traits each with an example from the play.

blocks.back: Lomov, Chubukov and Chubukov's daughter Natalya.

blocks.front: What are the two quarrels about?
blocks.back: Oxen Meadows, and whether Guess or Squeezer is the better dog.
Having the lower jaw shorter than the upper; Lomov says this of Squeezer.
Lomov and Natalya are engaged, but start quarrelling again; Chubukov calls for champagne.
